 HONOLULU (Island News) -- The Hawaii Department of Health (DOH) reported the 11th travel-related dengue fever case in the state this year.
 The infected person recently returned to Oahu after traveling to a region where dengue is common. There has been no connection found to any previous cases in Hawaii. 
 The expected risk of transmission is low due to circumstances surrounding this case. DOH teams were tasked to inspect mosquito control in the affected area. The community can help reduce the risk for any local transmission by exercising the best health practices.
 Mosquitoes need only small amounts of standing water which can lead to breeding grounds for mosquitoes. Breeding sites that are common include buckets, water-catching plants (such as bromeliads), small containers, planters, rain barrels and even cups left outside.
 Prevent mosquitoes from laying eggs by reducing standing water in homes and workplaces by pouring out containers. To learn more about mosquito control, visit health.hawaii.gov/vcb/mosquitoes .
 Dengue is a year-round risk found in the following tropical and subtropical areas: Central and South America, Asia (including the Republic of the Philippines), the Middle East, Africa and several Pacific Islands, such as U.S. territories like American Samoa, the Federated States of Micronesia, the Republic of the Marshall Islands and the Republic of Palau. Many popular tourist destinations within the Caribbean, including Puerto Rico, are affected by the disease.
 Travelers are advised to review current, country-specific travel information for guidance on dengue risk and prevention measures at least four to six weeks before traveling. Current travel health information and guidance can be found on the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) travel website .
 Dengue virus is spread from infected person to mosquito to person. While Hawaii is home to the type of mosquitoes that can carry dengue, the disease is not established in the state and cases are currently found only in travelers. Higher-than-normal dengue activity has been reported in multiple regions around the world.
 More information can be found on the Disease Outbreak Control Division website and Vector Control Branch website .
